blocks.text:
Design the core of a question-and-answer platform like Stack Overflow: users post questions, other users post answers, and the community votes answers (and questions) up or down. Every vote does double duty: it changes the post's visible score, and it changes the post author's reputation, a running score that gates certain privileges. Casting a downvote specifically requires the voter to have already earned enough reputation, and a question's author can mark one answer as accepted, which grants a further reputation bonus to both the answerer and the asker.

  • Actors: User (asks questions, posts answers, casts votes, accepts an answer), QAService (the core orchestrator).
  • Scope: question and answer posting, a vote-driven reputation system with a reputation-gated permission, and accepted-answer bonuses.

The distinguishing mechanic is a reputation system used as an earned, positive-currency permission gate, the inverse of Library Management System's fine-balance gate, which instead blocks an action once a penalty accumulates too high.
The system must support the following core capabilities:

items: Ask a question: a user posts a question with a title and body.
Post an answer: a user posts an answer to an existing question.
Vote: a user upvotes or downvotes a question or an answer, changing its score and the author's reputation.
Accept an answer: the question's author marks one answer as the accepted answer, granting a reputation bonus.
Reputation-gated downvoting: casting a downvote requires the voter to already hold a minimum amount of reputation.

blocks.text: Beyond correctness, the design should hold up along five quality pillars:

metadata.alt: Five non-functional pillars: scalability, extensibility, maintainability, performance, thread safety

items: Scalability: supporting many users, questions, answers, and votes must not require touching existing voting logic.
Extensibility: new reputation rules (a different point scheme, additional privilege thresholds) should plug in without rewriting the service.
Maintainability: reputation rules, notification, and post id creation are isolated in their own classes.
Performance: checking whether a user has already voted on a post is O(1) via a vote record lookup.
Thread safety: two votes on the same post submitted concurrently must not corrupt its score or double-count reputation.

blocks.text: Questions worth asking the interviewer before designing:

items: What is the exact reputation threshold required to cast a downvote?
Can a user change or retract their vote after casting it, or is a vote permanent once cast?
Should reputation ever decrease below a floor (for example, never below 1), or can it go arbitrarily low?
Can a question have more than one accepted answer, or is it strictly one at a time?
Should there be additional reputation-gated privileges beyond downvoting, such as editing others' posts or closing questions?

blocks.text: To keep the design focused, we make these explicit assumptions:

items: Downvoting requires a reputation of at least 125, matching the well-known real-world threshold this design is modeled after.
A vote is permanent once cast; a user cannot vote twice on the same post, and there is no retract or change-vote operation in this design.
A user cannot vote on their own question or answer.
A question has at most one accepted answer at a time; accepting a new answer would replace any previous acceptance (not implemented as a separate un-accept flow here, noted as a follow-up).

Reputation values are not floored at a minimum in this design; a very active downvoter with few of their own posts upvoted could theoretically go low, which real platforms typically guard against with a floor, noted in the improvements section.

blocks.text: The design centers on four core entities:

metadata.alt: Core entities: User, Question, Answer, VoteRecord

items: User: a member with a reputation score.
Question: a post with a title, body, score, and an optional accepted answer.
Answer: a post responding to a question, with its own score and an accepted flag.
VoteRecord: a record of one user's vote on one post, used to prevent duplicate voting.

blocks.text: These entities connect through a small set of well-defined relationships:

metadata.alt: A user authors many questions and answers and casts many vote records; a question receives many answers; a vote record references exactly one post

items: User to Question and User to Answer are both one-to-many.
Question to Answer is one-to-many.
User to VoteRecord is one-to-many, and each VoteRecord references exactly one question or answer.

blocks.text: Three patterns keep reputation rules, notification, and id generation decoupled from the core service.

Why needed: how many reputation points a vote or an accepted answer is worth is a policy decision (these exact numbers are famously stable in the real product this is modeled on, but a different site could reasonably tune them) that changes independently of the voting workflow itself.

metadata.alt: ReputationStrategy interface with StandardReputationStrategy point values for question upvotes, answer upvotes, downvotes, and accepted answers

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: a new point scheme is a new strategy implementation, with zero changes to QAService. What it solves: it isolates a frequently-debated policy (how much should this action be worth) from stable orchestration logic.
Why needed: votes cast, votes rejected, and answers accepted are all events a real Q&A platform would want to react to (reputation change notifications, badge awards, email digests).

metadata.alt: QAObserver interface notified by QAService on every lifecycle event

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: QAService does not need to know who is listening. What it solves: it decouples the core voting workflow from side effects.
Why needed: question ids and answer ids should not be generated ad hoc across calling code.

metadata.alt: PostIdFactory generating sequential Q and A prefixed ids

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: every question and answer is created through one consistent path. What it solves: centralizes id-generation rules so they cannot drift or collide.
Each class has a single, clear responsibility:

items: User: attributes userId, name, reputation; responsibility: track a member's earned standing.
Question: attributes questionId, authorId, title, score, acceptedAnswerId; responsibility: represent one asked question.
Answer: attributes answerId, questionId, authorId, score, isAccepted; responsibility: represent one answer to a question.
VoteRecord: attributes voterId, postId, voteType; responsibility: remember that a specific user has already voted on a specific post.
PostIdFactory: methods nextQuestionId, nextAnswerId; responsibility: generate sequential, correctly-prefixed ids.
QAService: the orchestrator; responsibility: validate and apply votes, process answer acceptance, and notify observers.

blocks.text: Two interfaces keep the design open for extension:

metadata.alt: ReputationStrategy and QAObserver interfaces with their key methods

items: ReputationStrategy: pointsForVote(postType, voteType) and pointsForAccept(role): abstract away exactly how many reputation points an action is worth.
QAObserver: onVoteCast / onVoteRejected / onAnswerAccepted: abstracts away who reacts to lifecycle events.

blocks.text: Three flows below cover a successful upvote, a downvote rejected for insufficient reputation, and an answer acceptance granting a dual reputation bonus.

metadata.alt: Carol upvotes Alice's question, increasing Alice's reputation by 5
Bob, with reputation below the 125 threshold, is rejected when trying to downvote an answer
Alice, the question author, accepts Bob's answer, granting Bob 15 reputation and Alice 2 reputation

blocks.text: The voting and acceptance workflows, alongside their rejection branches, look like this:

metadata.alt: Cast vote with self-vote, duplicate-vote, and reputation-threshold checks; accept answer with an authorization check and a dual reputation bonus

items: Vote path: cast vote → not a self-vote and not a duplicate → if downvote, reputation meets threshold → apply score and reputation changes.
Vote rejection paths: cast vote → self-vote or duplicate vote → rejected, or → downvote below reputation threshold → rejected.
Accept path: accept answer → caller is the question author → mark accepted, grant bonuses to both the answerer and the asker.
Accept rejection path: accept answer → caller is not the question author → rejected.

blocks.text: The service exposes a small, intention-revealing API:

items: castVote(voterId, postId, voteType): validates and applies a vote, or throws if disallowed.
acceptAnswer(callerId, questionId, answerId): marks an answer accepted and grants the reputation bonus, or throws if the caller is not the question's author.

blocks.text: Three custom exceptions cover the realistic failure modes:

items: VotingNotAllowedException: thrown for self-voting, duplicate voting, or attempting to downvote below the reputation threshold, carrying the specific reason.
UnauthorizedAcceptException: thrown when anyone other than the question's author tries to accept an answer.
InvalidPostException: thrown on an unknown question or answer id.

blocks.text: The critical race is two votes on the same post submitted at nearly the same moment.

metadata.alt: Two threads racing to vote on the same post; synchronization ensures one vote applies and records before the other is checked against the updated vote-record set

blocks.text: Synchronizing the duplicate-check-and-record step per post ensures a user cannot ever have two votes recorded on the same post, even under concurrent requests.
The pattern choices make several future features low-friction to add:

items: A new reputation scheme (a beta-site point structure, seasonal bonus events) is a new ReputationStrategy implementation.
A new notification channel (badges, email digests) is a new QAObserver implementation.
Additional reputation-gated privileges (editing others' posts, closing questions) can reuse the same threshold-check pattern established for downvoting.
Vote retraction can be added as a new service method without restructuring the existing vote-record model.
Single Responsibility: User tracks its own reputation, ReputationStrategy decides point values, QAObserver reacts to events, each for one reason to change.
Open/Closed: new reputation or notification behavior extends via new classes, not edits to QAService.
Liskov Substitution: any ReputationStrategy or QAObserver implementation can replace another without breaking the service.
Interface Segregation: QAObserver exposes only the three lifecycle callbacks a listener actually needs.
Dependency Inversion: QAService depends on the ReputationStrategy and QAObserver interfaces, not concrete classes.
A user with exactly 125 reputation is allowed to downvote, since the check is "at least" the threshold, not strictly greater.

A question author accepting an answer that was already accepted simply re-applies the same acceptance state (idempotent), rather than double-granting the bonus, since acceptance is checked before granting.
A user tries to vote on their own answer to someone else's question, still rejected as a self-vote regardless of whose question it is under.
Accepting a different answer on a question that already has an accepted answer replaces the previous acceptance.
castVote: O(1) for the self-vote check, the duplicate-vote lookup, and applying score and reputation changes.
acceptAnswer: O(1) to verify authorship and apply the dual reputation bonus.
Space: O(users + questions + answers + vote records) held in memory.

blocks.text: A relational schema mirrors the in-memory model directly, with foreign keys enforcing referential integrity:

metadata.alt: ER diagram: User, Question, Answer, VoteRecord

items: A unique index on VoteRecord(voterId, postId) enforces the one-vote-per-user-per-post rule directly at the database level.
An index on Answer(questionId) speeds up loading every answer for a given question.
Floor reputation at a minimum value (for example never below 1), matching how most real platforms guard against reputation going negative.
Support vote retraction, allowing a user to remove a previously cast vote.
Add additional reputation-gated privileges beyond downvoting, reusing the same threshold-check pattern.
Model a full badge and privilege-unlock system layered on top of the existing reputation tracking.

blocks.text: VoteType, User, Question, Answer, VoteRecord and PostIdFactory:
QAService, including the vote validation checks and the accept-answer workflow:

codes.python:
# Custom exceptions for the realistic failure modes.
class VotingNotAllowedException(Exception): pass
class UnauthorizedAcceptException(Exception): pass
class InvalidPostException(Exception): pass

# The core orchestrator tying every piece together.
class QAService:
    def __init__(self, reputation_strategy):
        self.users = {}          # userId -> User
        self.questions = {}      # questionId -> Question
        self.answers = {}        # answerId -> Answer
        self.vote_keys = set()    # voterId plus postId, for duplicate checks
        self.reputation_strategy = reputation_strategy  # pluggable point scheme
        self.observers = []        # listeners

    def add_user(self, user):
        self.users[user.user_id] = user  # register a user

    def add_question(self, question):
        self.questions[question.question_id] = question  # register a question

    def add_answer(self, answer):
        self.answers[answer.answer_id] = answer  # register an answer

    def add_observer(self, observer):
        self.observers.append(observer)  # register a listener

    def _author_of(self, post_id):
        if post_id in self.questions:
            return self.questions[post_id].author_id  # question author
        return self.answers[post_id].author_id           # answer author

    def _type_of(self, post_id):
        return "QUESTION" if post_id in self.questions else "ANSWER"  # distinguish post type

    def cast_vote(self, voter_id, post_id, vote_type):
        author_id = self._author_of(post_id)  # who owns this post
        if author_id == voter_id:               # self-vote check
            for obs in self.observers:
                obs.on_vote_rejected(voter_id, post_id, "Cannot vote on your own post")  # notify
            raise VotingNotAllowedException("Cannot vote on your own post")
        vote_key = f"{voter_id}|{post_id}"  # unique key for this voter and post
        if vote_key in self.vote_keys:        # duplicate-vote check
            for obs in self.observers:
                obs.on_vote_rejected(voter_id, post_id, "Already voted on this post")  # notify
            raise VotingNotAllowedException("Already voted on this post")
        voter = self.users[voter_id]  # look up voter
        if vote_type == VoteType.DOWNVOTE and voter.reputation < self.reputation_strategy.minimum_reputation_to_downvote():
            for obs in self.observers:
                obs.on_vote_rejected(voter_id, post_id, "Insufficient reputation to downvote")  # notify
            raise VotingNotAllowedException("Insufficient reputation to downvote")
        post_type = self._type_of(post_id)  # question or answer
        author_points = self.reputation_strategy.points_for_vote(post_type, vote_type)  # points for the author
        self.users[author_id].add_reputation(author_points)  # apply to author
        if vote_type == VoteType.DOWNVOTE:  # downvote costs the voter too
            voter.add_reputation(self.reputation_strategy.downvote_voter_cost())
        score_delta = 1 if vote_type == VoteType.UPVOTE else -1  # score always moves by 1
        if post_id in self.questions:
            self.questions[post_id].adjust_score(score_delta)  # adjust question score
        else:
            self.answers[post_id].adjust_score(score_delta)  # adjust answer score
        self.vote_keys.add(vote_key)  # record this vote
        for obs in self.observers:
            obs.on_vote_cast(post_id, voter_id, vote_type)  # notify

    def accept_answer(self, caller_id, question_id, answer_id):
        question = self.questions.get(question_id)  # look up question
        if question is None:
            raise InvalidPostException(f"Unknown question: {question_id}")
        if question.author_id != caller_id:  # must be the question's own author
            raise UnauthorizedAcceptException("Only the question author can accept an answer")
        answer = self.answers.get(answer_id)  # look up answer
        if answer is None:
            raise InvalidPostException(f"Unknown answer: {answer_id}")
        answer.is_accepted = True  # mark accepted
        question.accepted_answer_id = answer_id  # record on the question
        self.users[answer.author_id].add_reputation(self.reputation_strategy.points_for_accepted_answer_author())  # answerer bonus
        self.users[caller_id].add_reputation(self.reputation_strategy.points_for_accepting_asker())  # asker bonus
        for obs in self.observers:
            obs.on_answer_accepted(answer_id, question_id)  # notify

items: Why does casting a downvote cost the voter reputation as well as the author? Real Q&A platforms use this to discourage frivolous or hostile downvoting, since it is not entirely free for the person doing it either.

Why is the reputation threshold checked only for downvotes, not upvotes? Because upvoting has no meaningful potential for abuse in the same way, while downvoting a large volume of content could otherwise be used to harass another user with very little effort.

How would you extend this to support additional reputation-gated privileges, like editing others' posts? Add a new threshold constant and a new authorization check reusing the exact same pattern established for downvoting.

Fixed reputation thresholds vs a tiered privilege system: a single downvote threshold is simple to reason about and implement, at the cost of not modeling the fuller range of privileges (editing, closing, moderating) a real platform eventually needs, each with its own threshold.

No reputation floor vs a floor at a minimum value: allowing reputation to drop without a floor is simpler, at the cost of a heavy downvoter with few upvoted posts of their own theoretically dropping to an unusual, possibly confusing value; a real platform typically floors this at 1.

Single accepted answer vs multiple accepted answers: a single accepted answer per question is simpler and matches the well-known product this design is modeled on, though some Q&A platforms do experiment with multiple accepted answers for different sub-questions within one post.
Persist users, questions, answers, and vote records in a relational database rather than in-memory maps, using the schema in the Database Design section.
Emit vote and acceptance events to a message queue so downstream systems (badge awards, email digests, moderation queues) can consume them asynchronously instead of via in-process observers.
Add idempotency keys to castVote so retried network requests cannot double-apply a vote.
Expose metrics on downvote-rejection rate due to insufficient reputation, which can reveal whether the threshold is calibrated appropriately for the community's actual reputation distribution.
